Cab
KAB
n. (Hebrew)
Hebrew qāb, “a hollow vessel,” from a root meaning to be hollow; a small dry-measure equal to approximately 1/18 of an ephah (about 2 quarts or 2.1 liters). Appears once in Scripture, at the famine of Samaria in 2 Kings 6:25.

Biblical Definition

The cab is a Hebrew unit of dry measure, approximately 1/18 of an ephah (about 2 quarts in volume), mentioned only once in Scripture: at the famine of Samaria during the Syrian siege under Benhadad in 2 Kings 6:25. And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. The verse is one of the more grim in the OT narrative, illustrating the extremity of starvation in the besieged city: an ass’s head (normally unclean food, eaten only in desperation) sold for 80 silver pieces; a quarter-cab of dove’s dung (probably the indigestible plant-seed residue in the dung, or possibly a colloquial name for some inferior vegetable matter) sold for 5 silver pieces. The narrative continues with the most shocking incident of the famine: two women had agreed to boil and eat their children to survive; one woman boiled her son and ate him with the other; when the other woman hid her son rather than fulfilling her side of the agreement, the first appealed to the king for justice (2 Kgs 6:26-29). The king, learning the depth of the famine’s horror, tore his clothes and revealed the sackcloth he wore beneath. The cab in 2 Kings 6:25 is therefore a window into one of Scripture’s most somber narratives: the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness reaching the point of cannibalism within the besieged covenant city, with the smallest units of food sold at extortionate prices and the population reduced to eating what would never have been considered food in normal life. The narrative belongs to the larger biblical theology of covenant-curse: Deut 28:53-57 prophetically described exactly this kind of siege-cannibalism as among the most severe curses for covenant-breaking, and 2 Kings 6 records its fulfillment in the northern kingdom’s history. The cab as a unit therefore takes on, in its single biblical use, a structural-theological weight far beyond its small literal measurement: it is the measuring-unit of covenant judgment-extremity. Elisha’s subsequent prophecy in 2 Kings 7:1 (announcing the deliverance and the restoration of normal grain prices the next day) and its dramatic fulfillment through the Syrian retreat is the LORD’s answer to the famine and the demonstration that the same God who appoints siege also appoints deliverance.

Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) CAB: a small Hebrew dry-measure, approximately 1/18 of an ephah; mentioned once in Scripture, at the famine of besieged Samaria (2 Kgs 6:25), where a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung sold for five pieces of silver—a window into the severity of covenant-curse siege-famine and the LORD’s subsequent dramatic deliverance through Elisha.

CAB, n. — (Hebrew dry-measure.) Approximately 1/18 of an ephah, about 2 quarts. The single OT use is 2 Kings 6:25, in the famine of besieged Samaria.

FAMINE, n. — Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions; in scripture, often the consequence of covenant-unfaithfulness, with siege-famine being among the most severe of the covenant-curses prophetically described in Deut 28:53-57.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 6:25 — "And there was a great famine in Samaria: and, behold, they besieged it, until an ass’s head was sold for fourscore pieces of silver, and the fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver."

Deuteronomy 28:53 — "And thou shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters, which the LORD thy God hath given thee, in the siege, and in the straitness, wherewith thine enemies shall distress thee."

2 Kings 7:1 — "Then Elisha said, Hear ye the word of the LORD; Thus saith the LORD, To morrow about this time shall a measure of fine flour be sold for a shekel, and two measures of barley for a shekel, in the gate of Samaria."

2 Kings 6:30 — "And it came to pass, when the king heard the words of the woman, that he rent his clothes; and he passed by upon the wall, and the people looked, and, behold, he had sackcloth within upon his flesh."

Modern Corruption

The cab-narrative is corrupted in contemporary reading chiefly by being skipped past as obscure OT detail, missing the structural-covenantal substance of the famine-as-covenant-curse fulfillment and the dramatic deliverance through Elisha’s prophecy—and by the avoidance, in much contemporary preaching, of the somber siege-famine details that the OT records as the consequences of covenant unfaithfulness.

expand to see more

The 2 Kings 6 narrative is widely skipped in contemporary preaching as too somber, too gruesome, too disconnected from contemporary application—ass’s heads and dove’s dung and women cannibalizing their children belong, in the contemporary preacher’s judgment, to a register of OT horror that the modern congregation should be spared. Scripture includes the narrative, however, with deliberate purpose. It demonstrates the literal fulfillment of Deut 28:53-57’s covenant-curse prophecy; it shows the consequences of sustained covenant-unfaithfulness reaching the depths of siege-famine; it sets up the contrast with Elisha’s prophesied deliverance in chapter 7. The recovery is the recovery of biblical realism about covenant-consequences. The LORD’s holiness against sustained unfaithfulness is real; the prophesied judgments are not metaphorical but actual; the OT narrative records the historical fulfillment of the warnings the law had given. The contemporary application is sober: God’s covenant-people, then and now, are not exempt from the consequences of sustained unfaithfulness, and the contemporary pastor who avoids the somber OT narratives is hiding from the saints the warnings the Lord Himself recorded for their good.

The deeper pastoral substance includes the dramatic deliverance that follows. Elisha’s prophecy in 2 Kings 7:1 announces that the very famine that has reduced the people to extremity will be reversed the next day by the LORD’s action: a measure of fine flour for a shekel, two measures of barley for a shekel, normal prices restored at the gate. The deliverance comes through the most unexpected of means: four lepers, marginalized at the city gate, discover the empty Syrian camp (the LORD having frightened the Syrians with the sound of a great army and put them to flight); they bring back the news; the city is delivered overnight; Elisha’s prophecy is fulfilled to the day. The narrative pattern is one of the OT’s most pastorally consoling: even at the depth of covenant-curse’s extremity, the LORD’s deliverance can come in an hour, through means the besieged would never have imagined. Recover the somber narrative and recover the dramatic deliverance together; the doctrine that emerges is one of God’s holiness against sustained unfaithfulness paired with His mercy that overflows even at the depth of judgment’s consequences.

Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qāb (a hollow vessel, dry measure); approximately 1/18 of an ephah; mentioned once in Scripture, at the famine of besieged Samaria (2 Kgs 6:25)—a window into the covenant-curse siege-famine of Deut 28:53-57 and the dramatic deliverance through Elisha’s prophecy in 2 Kgs 7.

expand to see more

Hebrew qāb (H6894) — cab, a small dry-measure (the singular OT use, 2 Kgs 6:25).

Hebrew ’ēphāh (H374) — ephah (the larger standard against which the cab is measured; approximately 18 cabs).

Hebrew rā‘āb (H7458) — famine (the noun behind the siege-famine narrative).

Greek limos (G3042) — famine (the NT cousin term).

"The fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver—the cab’s singular OT use, illustrating the extremity of the Samaria siege-famine."

"The 2 Kgs 6 narrative demonstrates the literal fulfillment of the Deut 28:53-57 covenant-curse prophecy of siege-cannibalism."

"Contemporary preaching often skips the somber OT narratives; recovery is the biblical realism about covenant-consequences paired with the dramatic deliverance that follows in 2 Kgs 7."
